title: AES-128 Two earlier faults: full-key recovery (Piret–Quisquater 2003)

target.description: Full ten-round AES-128. Two useful byte faults before the round-8 diffusion constrain all sixteen last-round-key bytes, followed by AES-128 key-schedule inversion and verification of any surviving complete-key candidates.

setting.key_relation: One unchanged secret AES-128 master key; no related-key or key-schedule-fault oracle.
setting.key_population: AES-128 keys in the stated unprotected single-byte-fault model; no weak-key restriction.
setting.plaintext_model: A correct ciphertext and its faulty counterpart for each plaintext; different pairs may use different plaintexts. The source's algorithm associates every pair with the same key.

fault_model.target: A byte of the AES encryption state; faults in the key schedule are outside this result.
fault_model.granularity: One initial byte with an unknown nonzero difference; later diffusion may change four or sixteen state bytes.
fault_model.timing: After the round-7 diffusion layer and before the round-8 diffusion layer (theta_(R−3) to theta_(R−2)); theta is ShiftRows followed by MixColumns.
fault_model.location: The byte position is unknown. Propagation through two diffusion layers supplies information about all four last-round-key groups.
fault_model.value_control: The faulty byte value is random and assumed uniformly distributed; no chosen difference or bit-level fault control.
fault_model.sample_pairing: Every faulty ciphertext has its correct counterpart for the same plaintext and key; useful pairs are distinguished from total injection attempts.

assumptions: Only correct/faulty output pairs satisfying the stated single-byte model and timing window are counted.
The last-round-key candidate set is computed from differential constraints, and any remaining candidates require a separate check.
The paper instantiates and tests the 128-bit-block, 128-bit-key variant; its general extension remark is not a quantified AES-192/256 result.
The 77% statistic measures a singleton full-key candidate list before exhaustive verification of the remaining small list. It is not a universal 77% key-recovery probability.

In the source theta_r=ShiftRows_r followed by MixColumns_r. The four final-round-key groups in column-majorFIPSindices are{0,13,10,7}, {4,1,14,11}, {8,5,2,15}, {12,9,6,3}; these are affected sets, not ordered inverseMixColumns arguments.

time.reported: a few seconds on a PC
time.note: The timing is stated directly after the two-earlier-fault PC results on pp.84–85; processor details, trial count and precise timing protocol are not supplied.

data.note: Section 3.3 and Table 3 count two useful faults between theta_7 and theta_8, each with its correct ciphertext counterpart.

memory.note: Section 2 stores differential patterns D and candidate lists L but does not tabulate whole-attack peak memory.

preprocessing.note: Section 2 forms a table of 255*n single-byte-fault diffusion patterns. For one AES column n=4, this gives 1020 patterns as a derived component count, not a reported total preprocessing-time budget.

success.description: The PC experiments report a unique full-key candidate in 77% of cases. All reported remaining lists had at most sixteen candidates; trial count and numerical final verification success are unspecified. Giraud–Thillard Section3.2/footnote4 reports approximately92% for the same old two-useful-earlier-fault full-list uniqueness event in1,000,000 simulations, explicitly contrasting the original77%. Both observations are retained; neither is the measured probability of final key verification or physical fault acquisition.

review.scope: Verified only that the original77% and later92% are separately reported empirical singleton-list frequencies for the same old two-useful-earlier-fault algorithm. This source-attribution verification does not adjudicate their difference, establish a population rate, or certify final key verification/physical fault acquisition. Experimental protocol/raw-outcome reconciliation remains unresolved in /field_conflicts; the primary77% stays the original observation.

components.description: Later remeasurement: GT PDF5 Section3.2/footnote4 reports92% from1,000,000 simulations of the original extended D-filter with two useful earlier faults. Exact successful trial numerator, full sampling protocol and confidence interval are unavailable. Same list-uniqueness event as original77%; not an independent local factor or final-verified-output/acquisition yield.

evidence.interpretation: The two-pair attack, qualitative time, unique-candidate fraction and observed candidate-list cap keep separate meanings. Additional verification of survivors is not claimed to have a separately measured universal success rate.

evidence.locator: Complete PDF1–12/printed77–88, including Section2 model, Section3.3 every AESendpoint, Table3 and AppendixA.
evidence.interpretation: Exact12-page CHES2003 chapter independently read in full on2026-10-27. Reviewer finite component identities and arithmetic checks do not execute or reproduce the author attack or remeasure its empirical frequencies.

evidence.locator: PDF5 Section3.2/footnote4; PDF4 Section3.1; PDF5 Section3.3 separates the new S-filter.
evidence.interpretation: Direct later-author remeasurement of the same old full-list singleton event, at two useful earlier faults. The92% statement has a million-simulation denominator, unlike the original77%; no exact successful numerator is given. Preserve original77%, add later92% as an alternative observation and retain the disagreement. Do not treat0.98^4 as a proved independent product, or replace few-seconds native timing with the new one-fault eight-minute runtime.

limitations: Useful correct/faulty pairs exclude acquisition failures and faults outside the model; total physical attempts are not costed.
Computer experiments in this paper do not establish a measured physical fault-injection setup.
The reported rejection of mixed right/bad pairs is an observation with no trial count; it is not a proof that every physically malformed pair is rejected.

candidate_space.material: Complete 128-bit final-round key of AES-128, in bijection with the master key under inverse key expansion.

count.note: Section 3.3 says the full-key list never exceeded sixteen in the reported experiments. This upper bound is restricted to those observations, not all allowed faults.

field_conflicts.label: Full-key candidate-list uniqueness: original77% versus later92%
field_conflicts.description: Two reported experiments for the same original two-earlier-fault D-filter give different singleton-list frequencies. The later paper explicitly remeasures the old attack before introducing its new joint-column filter. Preserve both source observations; no protocol-level reconciliation or new experiment has been performed.

observations.reported: Unique whole-key candidate in77% of reported PC cases; trial count unspecified.

observations.locator: PDF5 Section3.2 and footnote4, before Section3.3.
observations.reported: Unique last-round-key candidate in92% of1,000,000 simulations; explicitly contrasts PQ03 Section3.3 value77%.
